🔗 Introduction and requirements

Hinglish samajh: URL shortener lambe web address ko chhota bana deta hai aur jab koi chhote link par click karta hai to use asli lambe URL par bhej deta hai. Teen kaam: shortening, redirecting aur high scalability. Requirements: short URL unique aur jitna ho sake chhota, roz 100 million URLs, 10 saal tak, read:write ratio 10:1, aur lagbhag 365 billion records. Repository ke notes mein storage 365 TB likha hai; meri jaanch ke hisaab se 100 bytes per record par ye 36.5 TB banta hai (aage estimation wale lesson mein samjhaya hai).

A URL shortener (like TinyURL or bit.ly) turns a very long web address into a short one. For example, https://www.example.com/products/shoes/running?color=blue&size=42&ref=newsletter becomes https://tinyurl.com/y7keocwj. When someone opens the short link, the service sends them to the original long address. Short links are easier to share in messages, print and social posts.

The main jobs of the service are URL shortening (create a short link for a long one), URL redirecting (send visitors from the short link to the long one) and high scalability (handle huge amounts of traffic). In this chapter we agree on these requirements: short URLs must be unique and as short as possible; the system must handle 100 million URL creations per day and keep working for 10 years; reads are far more common than writes with a read to write ratio of 10:1; and the total is about 365 billion records over 10 years (100 million x 365 days x 10 years).

The notes also say this needs "approximately 365 TB" of storage. I checked the arithmetic and explain it in the estimation lesson at the end: with about 100 bytes per record, 365 billion records need about 36.5 TB, so the 365 TB figure only works if each record is about 1 KB. Either way, the lesson is that the data is huge and needs a scalable database.

Requirements

RequirementValue
UniquenessEvery short URL is unique
LengthAs short as possible
Write volume100 million URLs per day
Lifetime10 years
Read to write ratio10 to 1 (reads dominate)
Records after 10 yearsabout 365 billion (100M x 365 x 10)

✨ Features

  • Create a short URL from a long one.
  • Redirect a short URL to the original.
  • Handle 100 million creations per day with a 10:1 read to write ratio.

✅ Benefits

  • Short links are easier to share and fit in limited spaces.
  • Links can be tracked for analytics.
  • Long, ugly URLs are hidden from users.

⚠️ Problems

  • Short links hide the destination, so they can be abused for phishing.
  • If the service goes down, all the links die.
  • The data set grows very large over time.

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · Introduction

This chapter discusses the design of a URL shortening service like TinyURL. The system's main goals include URL shortening, redirecting, and high scalability to handle large traffic volumes.

Requirements

  • Shortened URLs must be unique and as short as possible.
  • Handle 100 million URL generations per day with a 10-year support capacity.
  • Support efficient read operations with a 10:1 read-to-write ratio.
  • Store 365 billion records, requiring approximately 365 TB of storage over 10 years.

Interview questions and answers

What does a URL shortener do?
It maps a long URL to a short unique one, and redirects visitors who open the short URL to the long URL.
What are the main requirements?
Unique and short URLs, 100 million creations per day, 10 years of data, a read-heavy workload (10:1) and high scalability.
Cross question: How many records after 10 years?
100 million x 365 days x 10 years = 365 billion records.
Cross question: What risks does a URL shortener bring?
Short links can hide malicious sites, so a real service needs abuse detection, link scanning and rate limiting.

🛰️ High-level design: APIs and redirection (301 vs 302)

Hinglish samajh: Do API chahiye: shortening (POST api/v1/data/shorten, input longUrl, output shortURL) aur redirecting (GET short URL, jawab mein long URL par redirect). Redirect do tarah ke hote hain: 301 (hamesha ke liye, browser cache karta hai, server par load kam) aur 302 (asthayi, har visit service se guzarta hai, isliye click analytics aasan). Shortening ke liye hash function chahiye jo har long URL ko ek hash value de aur har hash value wapas long URL se jod sake.

We start with two REST-style APIs. The first is URL shortening: a client sends POST api/v1/data/shorten with the parameter {longUrl: longURLString}, and the server returns the shortURL. The second is URL redirecting: the client opens GET api/v1/shortUrl (in practice the short URL itself) and the server returns the longURL by redirecting the browser.

How does redirecting work? When you open a short link, the server answers with an HTTP redirect, and the browser then jumps to the long URL given in the Location header. There are two kinds of redirect, and the choice matters. A 301 redirect means "moved permanently". The browser caches the answer, so later requests for the same short URL go straight to the long URL and never reach the shortener again. This reduces the server load. A 302 redirect means "moved temporarily". The browser does not cache it, so every visit goes through the shortener first, which is useful when you want to track clicks for analytics.

For shortening, the core idea is to use a hash function that maps each long URL to a short value (the "hash value"). The function must satisfy two rules: each long URL maps to exactly one hash value, and each hash value can be mapped back to the long URL (through our database). We design this function in the next lessons.

How it works, step by step

  1. A client creates a short URL with a POST request to the shorten endpoint.
  2. The service returns the short URL.
  3. A visitor opens the short URL with a GET request.
  4. The service looks up the long URL and replies with a 301 or 302 redirect.
  5. The browser follows the Location header to the long URL.

API endpoints

PurposeMethod and pathInputOutput
Shorten a URLPOST api/v1/data/shorten{longUrl: longURLString}shortURL
RedirectGET api/v1/shortUrlthe short URLlongURL (via HTTP redirect)

301 vs 302 redirect

Point301 Moved Permanently302 Found (temporary)
Browser cachingBrowser caches the redirectNot cached
Server loadLower, repeat visits skip the serviceHigher, every visit hits the service
Click analyticsHard (you miss repeat visits)Easy (you see every visit)
Best whenReducing load matters mostTracking clicks matters most

✨ Features

  • Two APIs: shorten and redirect.
  • 301 (permanent, cached) or 302 (temporary, trackable).
  • A hash function maps long URLs to short values.

✅ Benefits

  • A very small API surface.
  • The 301 or 302 choice lets you balance load against analytics.
  • Standard HTTP behaviour that every browser understands.

⚠️ Problems

  • With 301, you lose visibility of repeat visits.
  • With 302, every visit adds load on the service.
  • The hash function must avoid collisions.

Original notes from the repository

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · Step 1: High-Level Design

API Endpoints

  1. URL Shortening:
    • Endpoint: POST api/v1/data/shorten
    • Parameters: {longUrl: longURLString}
    • Returns: shortURL
  2. URL Redirecting:
    • Endpoint: GET api/v1/shortUrl
    • Returns: longURL for redirection.

URL Redirection

  • 301 Redirect: A 301 redirect shows that the requested URL is “permanently” moved to the long URL. The browser caches the response, and subsequent requests for the same URL will not be sent to the URL shortening service.
  • 302 Redirect: Temporary; useful for analytics like tracking clicks.

URL Shortening

  • Use a hash function to generate a short URL, mapping long URLs to unique shortened versions.
  • The hash function must satisfy the following requirements:
    • Each longURL must be hashed to one hashValue.
    • Each hashValue can be mapped back to the longURL.

Interview questions and answers

What is the difference between 301 and 302?
301 is a permanent redirect that browsers cache, which reduces server load. 302 is temporary and not cached, so each visit passes through the shortener, which allows click analytics.
Which would you choose for a service that sells analytics?
302, because every visit must reach the service so it can be counted.
Cross question: Which reduces cost more?
301, because repeat visits skip the service entirely.
What are the two API endpoints?
POST api/v1/data/shorten with the long URL returns the short URL; GET on the short URL returns a redirect to the long URL.

🗃️ The data model

Hinglish samajh: Short URL se long URL ka mapping store karna hai. 365 billion records memory mein nahi aa sakte, isliye relational database use karte hain jisme table mein id (primary key), shortURL aur longURL hote hain. Redirect ke liye shortURL par index zaroori hai. Baad mein replication aur sharding se table ko bada kiya ja sakta hai, aur hot links ko cache mein rakha jaata hai.

We need to store the mapping from short URL to long URL. A first idea is to keep everything in a hash table in memory, but memory is limited and expensive, and we would have 365 billion records. So we store the mappings in a relational database, which can hold the data on disk and keeps memory for caching the hot records.

The table is very simple. It has an id (the primary key), the shortURL and the longURL. Think of each row as one link. The database can be scaled later with replication and sharding, because rows do not depend on each other and are always looked up by their key.

One more design choice: the short URL should have an index so that redirect lookups (the 90% case) are fast. Also, to avoid creating duplicate short links for the same long URL, the shortening flow first checks whether the long URL already exists (we will see this in the flow lesson).

The URL table

ColumnType (example)Meaning
idBIGINT (primary key)Unique ID from the ID generator
shortURLVARCHAR(7)The short code, for example zn9edcu
longURLVARCHAR(2048)The original long URL

The table in SQL

CREATE TABLE url (
  id        BIGINT       PRIMARY KEY,      ␀class="nu">0␀
  short_url VARCHAR(class="nu">7)   NOT NULL UNIQUE,  ␀class="nu">1␀
  long_url  VARCHAR(class="nu">2048) NOT NULL
);

␀class="nu">2␀
SELECT long_url FROM url WHERE short_url = 'zn9edcu';

␀class="nu">3␀
SELECT short_url FROM url WHERE long_url = 'https:␀class="nu">4␀

✨ Features

  • A relational table with id, shortURL and longURL.
  • Index on the short URL for fast lookups.
  • Rows are independent, so the table can be sharded later.

✅ Benefits

  • Simple and well understood.
  • Persistent and not limited by memory.
  • Easy to replicate and shard by key.

⚠️ Problems

  • Disk-based lookups are slower than memory, so a cache is needed for hot links.
  • A very large table needs partitioning and good indexes.
  • Checking if a long URL exists needs an index on longURL too.

Store <shortURL, longURL> mappings in a relational database to optimize memory usage. The table schema includes:

Interview questions and answers

How would you store the URL mappings?
In a relational table with an id, the short URL and the long URL, indexed on the short URL. It can be replicated and sharded as it grows.
Why not keep everything in memory?
There could be hundreds of billions of records, which is too much for memory. Keep the hot ones in a cache and the rest on disk.
Cross question: Would a NoSQL key-value store also work?
Yes. The access pattern is simple (get by key), so a key-value store fits well too. The relational choice is a reasonable default.
Cross question: What index do you need?
A unique index on the short URL for redirects, and an index on the long URL to find existing links quickly (or a hash of it).

#️⃣ The hash function: base 62 conversion vs hash and collision resolution

Hinglish samajh: Short code ke liye 62 characters (0-9, a-z, A-Z) lete hain. 7 characters se 62^7, yaani lagbhag 3.5 trillion combinations milte hain jo 365 billion URLs ke liye kaafi hain. Do tareeke: (1) base 62 conversion: har URL ko unique numeric ID do (chapter 7 ka ID generator) aur use base 62 mein badlo, jaise 2009215674938 se zn9edcu; isme collision nahi hota par agla URL guess karna aasan ho sakta hai. (2) Hash + collision resolution: CRC32, MD5 ya SHA-1 ke pehle 7 characters lo, collision ho to string jodkar dobara hash karo, aur Bloom filter se check tez karo.

The heart of the design is how to turn a long URL into a short code. We use a code of 7 characters, and we must make sure there are enough combinations. How many do we need? We expect 365 billion URLs. If the code uses the 62 characters 0-9, a-z, A-Z, then 7 characters give 62^7 = about 3.5 trillion different codes (3,521,614,606,208 exactly). That is far more than 365 billion, so 7 is the right length. (6 characters would only give about 56.8 billion, which is too few.)

Option 1: base 62 conversion. Give every URL a unique numeric ID (from the distributed ID generator of chapter 7) and convert that number into base 62, the same way you convert a number to binary or hexadecimal. For example, the ID 2009215674938 becomes zn9edcu in base 62. The result is unique because the IDs are unique. (I verified this conversion with code.) The code length is not fixed: small IDs give short codes.

Option 2: hash and resolve collisions. Run the long URL through a hash function such as CRC32, MD5 or SHA-1. These produce long values (CRC32 gives 8 hex characters), so we take only the first 7 characters. But different URLs can then give the same 7 characters, which is a collision. To resolve it, we check the database; if the short code already exists for another URL, we append a predefined string to the long URL and hash again, repeating until there is no collision. This works but can be expensive because of repeated database queries. A Bloom filter (a compact structure that quickly says "definitely not present" or "maybe present") can cut down those database checks.

Which one to choose? The comparison table shows the trade-offs. In this chapter we pick base 62 conversion because it never collides, as long as the ID generator is unique. Its downside is that the next short URL is easy to guess if IDs increase by 1, which can be a security concern, so some designs add randomness or a shuffling step.

Hash plus collision resolution vs base 62 conversion

PointHash + collision resolutionBase 62 conversion
Short URL lengthFixed (for example 7 characters)Not fixed, grows with the ID
Needs a unique ID generatorNoYes
CollisionsPossible, must be resolvedNot possible
Guessing the next URLNot possible, it does not depend on an IDEasy if IDs go up by 1 (a security concern)

How many codes can each length hold?

LengthCombinations (62^n)Enough for 365 billion URLs?
656,800,235,584 (about 56.8 billion)No
73,521,614,606,208 (about 3.5 trillion)Yes
8218,340,105,584,896 (about 218 trillion)Yes, but longer than needed

Base 62 conversion in code (C#)

const string Alphabet = ␀class="nu">3␀;

static string ToBase62(long id)
{
    if (id == class="nu">0) return ␀class="nu">4␀;
    var sb = new StringBuilder();
    while (id > class="nu">0)
    {
        sb.Insert(class="nu">0, Alphabet[(int)(id % class="nu">62)]);   ␀class="nu">0␀
        id /= class="nu">62;
    }
    return sb.ToString();
}

static long FromBase62(string s)
{
    long n = class="nu">0;
    foreach (char c in s) n = n * class="nu">62 + Alphabet.IndexOf(c);
    return n;
}

Console.WriteLine(ToBase62(class="nu">2009215674938));   ␀class="nu">1␀
Console.WriteLine(FromBase62(␀class="nu">5␀));     ␀class="nu">2␀

✨ Features

  • 62 characters: 0-9, a-z, A-Z.
  • 7 characters give about 3.5 trillion codes.
  • Two options: base 62 conversion, or hash with collision resolution.

✅ Benefits

  • Base 62: no collisions and an easy design if you have an ID generator.
  • Hash approach: fixed length and no ID generator needed.
  • A Bloom filter reduces database checks in the hash approach.

⚠️ Problems

  • Base 62: needs a unique ID generator, and the next URL can be guessed.
  • Hash approach: collisions must be detected and resolved, which costs time.
  • Taking only 7 characters of a hash makes collisions more likely than the full hash.

Original notes from the repository

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · Hash Function + Comparison

1. Base 62 Conversion:
  • Encodes numbers using characters [0-9, a-z, A-Z], providing 62 possible characters.
  • Base conversion is another approach commonly used for URL shorteners.
  • A unique id can be assigned to the short url and ID can be base 62 converted to get the short URL.
  • A 7-character hash supports up to 3.5 trillion unique URLs, enough for 365 billion URLs.

Example: Convert ID 2009215674938 to Base 62:

  • 2009215674938 → zn9edcu.
2. Hash + Collision Resolution:
  • Use hash functions like CRC32, MD5, or SHA-1.
  • One approach is to collect the first 7 characters of a hash value; however, this method can lead to hash collisions.
  • To resolve collisions,recursively append a new predefined string until no more collision but this can be expensive.
  • Resolve collisions with Bloom Filters for efficient lookup.
  • Hash + Collision Resolution:
    • Fixed short URL length
    • Does not need a unique ID generator
    • Collision is possbile and needs resolution
    • Not possible to find the next available short URL because it does not depend on ID
  • Base 62 Conversion
    • The length is not fixed and goes up with ID
    • It needs a unique ID generator
    • Collision is not possbile
    • Easy to find the next short URL if ID increments by 1 (Can be a security concern)

Interview questions and answers

Why 7 characters?
62^7 is about 3.5 trillion, which is more than the 365 billion URLs we need. 62^6 is only about 56.8 billion, which is too few.
How does base 62 conversion work?
Give each URL a unique numeric ID and convert it to base 62, using the characters 0-9, a-z and A-Z. For example 2009215674938 becomes zn9edcu.
How do you resolve collisions in the hash approach?
Check whether the 7-character value is already used. If so, append a predefined string to the long URL and hash again until there is no collision. A Bloom filter speeds up the check.
Cross question: Which approach do you prefer and why?
Base 62, because collisions are impossible with a unique ID generator and the logic is simple. The cost is dependence on the ID generator and guessable sequential URLs.
Cross question: How would you stop people from guessing the next short URL?
Do not hand out strictly sequential IDs: for example shuffle the bits of the ID, add a random component, or use a keyed permutation before the base 62 conversion.

➕ The URL shortening flow

Hinglish samajh: Shortening flow: pehle long URL aata hai; check karte hain ki wo database mein pehle se hai ya nahi. Hai to wahi short URL wapas. Nahi hai to distributed ID generator se unique ID lete hain, use base 62 mein badalkar short URL banate hain, aur (id, shortURL, longURL) database mein save karke short URL wapas dete hain. Do ek saath aane wali same requests ke liye database par unique constraint lagana chahiye.

Now we can describe exactly what happens when someone submits a long URL. The service follows five steps. First, it receives the long URL. Second, it checks whether the long URL already exists in the database. If it does, the service simply returns the existing short URL (we do not want two short links for the same page). Third, if the long URL is new, the service generates a unique ID using the distributed unique ID generator. Fourth, it converts the ID to a short URL using base 62. Fifth, it stores the mapping (id, shortURL, longURL) in the database and returns the short URL.

Look at the example in the notes. The ID 2009215674938 is converted to the short URL "zn9edcu", and the row (2009215674938, zn9edcu, the long URL) is saved. This design combines two things you learned earlier: the unique ID generator (chapter 7) and base 62 conversion (the last lesson).

A few real-world details are worth mentioning: the existence check should use an index on the long URL (or on a hash of it) so that it is fast; two requests for the same new URL at the same instant might both pass the check, so the database needs a unique constraint to stay safe; and the response should be quick, since users are waiting.

How it works, step by step

  1. Receive the long URL.
  2. Check whether it already exists in the database.
  3. If it exists, return its existing short URL.
  4. Otherwise generate a unique ID with the ID generator.
  5. Convert the ID to a short URL with base 62.
  6. Save the id, short URL and long URL in the database and return the short URL.

The shortening flow in code (C#)

public string Shorten(string longUrl)
{
    ␀class="nu">0␀
    var existing = db.FindShortUrl(longUrl);
    if (existing != null) return existing;

    ␀class="nu">1␀
    long id = idGenerator.NextId();          ␀class="nu">2␀
    string shortUrl = ToBase62(id);          ␀class="nu">3␀

    ␀class="nu">4␀
    db.Insert(new UrlRow { Id = id, ShortUrl = shortUrl, LongUrl = longUrl });
    return shortUrl;
}

✨ Features

  • Existence check before creating.
  • ID generator plus base 62.
  • Mapping stored in the database.

✅ Benefits

  • No duplicate short links for the same long URL.
  • No collisions because IDs are unique.
  • Simple, linear flow that is easy to test.

⚠️ Problems

  • The existence check adds a database lookup to every write.
  • Races between identical requests need a unique constraint.
  • The ID generator is a critical dependency.

Original notes from the repository

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · URL Shortening Flow

  1. Check if longURL exists in the database.
  2. If found, return the existing shortURL.
  3. Otherwise:
    • Generate a unique ID using a distributed ID generator.
    • Convert the ID to shortURL using Base 62.
    • Store the <id, shortURL, longURL> mapping in the database.

Interview questions and answers

Walk me through shortening a URL.
Check if the long URL exists; if so, return its short URL. If not, get a unique ID from the ID generator, convert it to base 62, store the mapping, and return the short URL.
Why check for an existing long URL first?
So that one long URL does not receive many short URLs, which wastes space and complicates analytics.
Cross question: What if two requests for the same new URL arrive together?
Both could pass the check. Add a unique constraint on the long URL (or its hash) so one insert fails and the service returns the existing record.
Cross question: What if the ID generator is down?
Shortening fails, so run the ID generator with redundancy and failover, as discussed in chapter 7. Redirects keep working because they do not need it.

↪️ The URL redirecting flow

Hinglish samajh: Redirect flow mein kyunki reads zyada hain, ise sabse tez hona chahiye. User short URL par click karta hai, request load balancer ke raste web server tak jaati hai, server pehle cache mein mapping dhundta hai, nahi mile to database se leta hai aur cache mein bhar deta hai, aur phir user ko long URL par redirect kar deta hai. Popular links cache se hi mil jaate hain, isse database par load bahut kam ho jaata hai.

Since reads are ten times more common than writes, the redirect path must be as fast as possible. The flow has three steps. First, a user clicks a short URL, for example https://tinyurl.com/zn9edcu. The request goes through a load balancer to one of the web servers. Second, the web server looks up the mapping: it checks the cache first, because the same popular links are requested again and again, and only if the short URL is not in the cache does it query the database. After finding it in the database, it stores the result in the cache for next time. Third, the server redirects the user to the long URL.

This is the cache-aside pattern from chapter 1. Because a small share of links gets most of the traffic (viral links), a cache with a good hit rate removes most reads from the database. If the short URL does not exist in the cache or the database, the server returns a "not found" response.

Remember the 301/302 choice here: with 301 the browser caches the redirect itself and does not even come back, which saves even more traffic; with 302 every click arrives at our servers and can be counted.

How it works, step by step

  1. A user clicks the short URL.
  2. The load balancer sends the request to a web server.
  3. The server looks for the short URL in the cache.
  4. On a cache miss it queries the database and fills the cache.
  5. The server redirects the user to the long URL (or returns not found).

The redirect flow in code (C#)

public IActionResult Redirect(string shortUrl)
{
    ␀class="nu">0␀
    var longUrl = cache.Get(shortUrl);
    if (longUrl == null)
    {
        ␀class="nu">1␀
        longUrl = db.FindLongUrl(shortUrl);
        if (longUrl == null) return NotFound();
        cache.Set(shortUrl, longUrl, TimeSpan.FromHours(class="nu">24));
    }
    ␀class="nu">2␀
    return Redirect302(longUrl);
}

✨ Features

  • Cache before database.
  • Stateless web servers behind a load balancer.
  • 301 or 302 redirect response.

✅ Benefits

  • Fast redirects for popular links.
  • Database load is small because of the cache.
  • Easy to scale web servers horizontally.

⚠️ Problems

  • Cache misses are slower and hit the database.
  • Stale cache entries if a link is deleted or changed.
  • A cache failure sends all traffic to the database.

Original notes from the repository

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · URL Redirecting Flow

  1. User clicks a shortURL.
  2. Query <shortURL, longURL> mapping:
    • Check the cache first for faster access.
    • If not in the cache, query the database.
  3. Redirect the user to longURL.

Interview questions and answers

Describe the redirect flow.
The user clicks the short URL; a web server checks the cache for the mapping; on a miss it queries the database and caches the result; then it redirects the user to the long URL.
Why use a cache here?
The workload is read-heavy (10:1) and a small set of links is very popular, so a cache gives a high hit rate and protects the database.
Cross question: What if a short URL expires or is deleted?
Delete it from the database and from the cache (or use a TTL) so that visitors get a not-found response instead of an old redirect.
Cross question: What happens if the cache goes down?
Requests fall back to the database, which may be overloaded. Use several cache nodes, replication and rate limiting to protect the database.

🧰 Additional considerations: abuse, scaling, analytics, availability

Hinglish samajh: Design poora karne ke liye char extra baatein: (1) rate limiter, taaki koi shortening API ka galat istemal na kare; (2) scalability: web tier stateless hai isliye servers jod sakte hain, database tier mein replication aur sharding; (3) analytics: click rate, source, time ka data business ke liye kaam aata hai (302 redirect aur queue se); (4) high availability aur reliability: replication aur multiple data centers se links kabhi na tootein.

To finish the design, the notes list four extra topics. The first is the rate limiter. A malicious user could send a huge number of shortening requests and fill our database or exhaust our ID range. A rate limiter (chapter 4) can limit requests per IP address or API key. It protects the service from abuse.

The second is scalability. The web tier is stateless, so it scales simply by adding or removing web servers. The database tier uses replication (for more read capacity and safety) and sharding (to split the 365 billion records), as in chapters 1 and 5. A cache protects the database from hot reads.

The third is analytics. Data such as how often a link is clicked, the source of the click and the time is valuable for business insights. This is one reason to prefer 302 redirects, because the service sees every click. Record click events asynchronously, for example through a message queue, so that analytics never slows down redirects.

The fourth is high availability and reliability. The system should keep working through failures: replicate the database, run several instances of every component in more than one data center, and keep the unique ID generator highly available. A short URL that fails to open is a broken link for the customer, so reliability matters a lot.

  • Analytics storage can grow faster than the URL data.
  • Sharding makes some queries (like the long URL existence check) harder.

Original notes from the repository

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · Additional Considerations

Rate Limiter

  • Prevent abuse by setting limits on requests per IP.

Scalability

  1. Web Tier: Stateless, scalable by adding/removing web servers.
  2. Database Tier: Use replication and sharding.

Analytics

  • Collect data like click rates, source, and timestamps for business insights.

High Availability and Reliability

  • Ensure consistent and reliable services using database replication and fault-tolerant design.

Interview questions and answers

How do you scale the URL shortener?
Make the web tier stateless and add servers, use a cache for hot links, replicate the database for reads and availability, and shard it for volume.
How do you prevent abuse?
Use a rate limiter per IP or API key, and consider scanning submitted URLs for malware or phishing.
Cross question: How do you collect analytics without slowing redirects?
Send click events to a message queue and process them asynchronously; use 302 redirects so each click reaches the service.
Cross question: How would you keep the service highly available?
Run redundant instances in several data centers, replicate data, make the ID generator fault tolerant, and monitor everything.

🧮 Back-of-the-envelope estimation and a storage check

Hinglish samajh: Estimation: 100 million writes per din / 86,400 second = lagbhag 1,160 writes per second, aur 10:1 ratio se reads lagbhag 11,600 per second. 10 saal mein 100M x 365 x 10 = 365 billion records. 100 bytes per record par storage 36.5 TB banta hai; repository mein 365 TB likha hai jo tab sahi hoga jab har record lagbhag 1 KB ka ho. Assumption saaf likhna zaroori hai. 62^7 lagbhag 3.5 trillion hai, yaani 7 characters kaafi hain. Ye lesson meri taraf se jodha gaya hai.

Let us apply chapter 2 to this design. (This lesson is my own addition, using the numbers from the notes.) Writes: 100 million creations per day divided by 86,400 seconds in a day gives about 1,160 writes per second. Reads: with a 10:1 read to write ratio, reads are about 11,600 per second. These numbers are easy to handle with a few web servers and a cache, so the design pressure is mostly on storage, not on traffic.

Number of records: 100 million per day x 365 days x 10 years = 365 billion records. Storage: the notes say about 365 TB. Let us check. If an average record (the long URL, the short code and the id) is about 100 bytes, then 365 billion x 100 bytes = 36.5 x 10^12 bytes = 36.5 TB. To reach 365 TB you would need about 1 KB per record. A common mistake is to multiply by 10 years twice: the 365 billion records already include the 10 years. So state your assumption (bytes per record) clearly. Both numbers are far too big for one server, so partitioning and replication are needed (with 3 copies, 36.5 TB becomes about 110 TB).

Code length: 62^7 is about 3.5 trillion, about 9.6 times more than the 365 billion URLs we need, so 7 characters leave comfortable room. Estimation is a good time to catch inconsistencies in the numbers you are given, and doing it calmly shows interviewers that you check your work.

The estimates

QuantityCalculationResult
Write QPS100,000,000 / 86,400about 1,160 per second
Read QPS (10:1)1,160 x 10about 11,600 per second
Records in 10 years100M x 365 x 10365 billion
Storage at 100 bytes per record365 billion x 100 B36.5 TB
Storage if a record is 1 KB365 billion x 1 KB365 TB
Storage with 3 copies (100 B records)36.5 TB x 3about 110 TB
Code space with 7 characters62^7about 3.5 trillion

The estimates in Python

writes_per_day = 100_000_000
write_qps = writes_per_day / 86_400            ␀class="nu">0␀
read_qps = write_qps * class="nu">10                      ␀class="nu">1␀
records = writes_per_day * class="nu">365 * class="nu">10            ␀class="nu">2␀
storage_tb_100b = records * class="nu">100 / 1e12         ␀class="nu">3␀
storage_tb_1kb = records * class="nu">1000 / 1e12         ␀class="nu">4␀
codes_7 = class="nu">62 ** class="nu">7                              ␀class="nu">5␀

print(round(write_qps), round(read_qps), records, storage_tb_100b, storage_tb_1kb, codes_7)

✨ Features

  • QPS from daily volume.
  • Record count from years of data.
  • Storage from bytes per record, with the assumption stated.

✅ Benefits

  • Shows that traffic is modest but storage is large.
  • Justifies replication, sharding and caching.
  • Demonstrates careful arithmetic.

⚠️ Problems

  • The average record size is an assumption.
  • Peak traffic can be several times the average.
  • Replication multiplies storage.

Interview questions and answers

Estimate the QPS for the URL shortener.
About 1,160 writes per second (100 million per day divided by 86,400) and about 11,600 reads per second with a 10:1 ratio. Peak is higher, say double.
How much storage is needed over 10 years?
About 365 billion records. At about 100 bytes each that is 36.5 TB; the notes quote 365 TB, which would need about 1 KB per record. I would state the assumption and design for tens to hundreds of TB with replication.
Cross question: Why did you question the 365 TB figure?
Because 365 billion x 100 bytes is 36.5 TB. Multiplying by 10 years again would double count the time. Checking the arithmetic is part of a good estimate.
Cross question: What do these numbers tell you about the design?
Traffic is manageable with a cache and several stateless servers, but the data volume requires a replicated and sharded storage layer.
